key_insight: Disorder and topological vortices in the optical dipole phase can work together to amplify bulk photovoltaic currents, with the effect controlled by material topology, defect symmetry, and light polarization.
engineering_relevance: The paper suggests a route to boost solar-response signals in topological materials by tuning frequency and defect design, offering a new knob for photovoltaic device engineering.
method: Analyzes optical dipole matrix-element phase singularities (Berry-phase vortices) in topological materials.
Models electron-impurity skew scattering from real-space defects to predict enhanced ballistic photovoltaic current.
Applies the framework to multifold fermions, Weyl semimetals, and 2D Dirac systems to derive frequency scaling and tensor constraints.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical case studies and predicted frequency exponents/tensor selection rules, but not experimental measurements or benchmark performance data.
watch_item: The predicted enhancement depends on specific topology and defect symmetries, so real devices may need precise defect characterization and controlled fabrication to realize the effect.
paper_title: Vortex-enhanced photovoltaic current in disordered topological materials
